x: Wafer filters Right-click a wafer in the Deck to choose what it accepts. A wafer with no filters accepts everything. Rules Each filter is a row. A row can match an Item, a Tag or a Mod ID (a Fluid on a fluid wafer), and it can Allow or Deny. The first enabled row that matches decides. An item gets in only if that row says Allow. Rows can be switched off, moved up or down, or removed. With filters on, items that match no row stay out. Filling order Wafers fill from left to right. When several kinds arrive together, the higher Allow rows take space first. Empty out The same window has an Empty out button. It moves everything on that wafer onto the Deck's other wafers, and each item costs the usual charge. Nothing is ever destroyed this way. What finds no room stays where it is.

Making chips by hand Nearly every JASM recipe is built from chips. Logic and Memory Chips need nothing but a few common blocks. Step by step Cut a Data Crystal into a Blank Chip at a Stonecutter. Cook the Blank Chip. On a Campfire it becomes an Unquenched Logic Chip ; in a Blast Furnace, an Unquenched Memory Chip. Drop the hot chip in water, still or flowing. After 2 seconds (by default) it hisses and becomes a Logic Chip or a Memory Chip. The whole stack cools at once, and no water is used up. Other chips Link Chips and Advanced chips can only be made by a Bitling in the Chip Workshop. Find out more. In bulk The Crystal Foundry makes Blank Chips straight from Crystal Seeds.

Link Chip The chip for the third tier of JASM. A Link Chip can only be made by a Bitling in the Chip Workshop. It can't be crafted by hand. What it is for Eight Data Cables round a Link Chip make eight Advanced Data Cables. Third-tier recipes need it, like the Advanced Deck, the 16K wafers and the Access Port. Hand one to a wild Bitling to make friends. A Link Bitling is made from eight of them.

Nibblings and Bytelings The grown-up stages of a Bitling. Each one works the Chip Workshop better than the last. Nibbling Makes only its own chip type, and Advanced chips more often. Battery of 200,000 FE. Needs 300 chips of training to grow up. Byteling Makes only its own type. A switch in the Workshop picks standard or Advanced chips. Battery of 400,000 FE. The only critter that can build a Synapse Core. Recipes

Power Upgrade A port with a Power Upgrade supplies FE to the machine it faces. It is how a furnace or a modded machine gets power from your network. Every port has a slot for it: Access Ports and item ports. The power comes from the network, so keep a generator on it. Recipe

Demolition Bay A Demolition Bay breaks the block in front of it into its own grid, scoops up fluids and picks up items that land on its face. A Bitling in welding goggles works the laser. Enchant it like a pickaxe for Fortune, Silk Touch and Efficiency. At a glance Speed 2 seconds, down to half a second with 3 Speed Upgrades Breaking 6 FE for each point of cost: 1, plus the block's hardness and drops, times enchantments Scooping 50 FE a bucket Holds 10,000 FE and 16 buckets Good to know An Input Port empties it. It runs on cable power and doesn't take up a place on the machine limit. With a Redstone Upgrade it can work once for each redstone pulse. Its opposite is the Deployment Bay. Recipe

Wrench For turning machines and picking them up. Right-click a side of a JASM machine, Archive or generator to turn its front there. Sneak and right-click a JASM machine, cable or power block to pick it up at once. It keeps what it keeps when mined. Wrenches from other mods work on JASM blocks too, and this one works with mods that accept any wrench. Recipe Four Data Crystals in a line.

Data Cables Data Cables join your crafting blocks into one network and carry power between them. Any two cables join, whatever the tier. Cable Power it moves Made from Data Cable 1,000 FE a tick iron, redstone and an amethyst shard Advanced 10,000 FE a tick 8 Data Cables round a Link Chip Elite 50,000 FE a tick 8 Advanced round an Advanced Link Chip Each recipe makes 8 cables. Good to know Every cable passes power on at its own speed, so a slower cable only slows the power that goes through it. Machines that simply touch each other form a network too, with no cable at all. Different players' networks never join. Cables don't count toward the machine limit. A cable can carry up to six thin Access Ports, one on each face. See networks for the rules in full. Recipes

Mechanics How things work, rather than what things are. The pages follow the order you will need them. Crystals and chips Growing Data Crystals Making chips by hand Bitlings Befriending Bitlings Training Bitlings Storage How storage works Wafer filters Backups and recovery Sending items to players Networks and power Networks Co-op play Power Autocrafting Autocrafting Crafting rules

Recipe Rack A Recipe Rack holds 16 filled Recipe Cards. Every Crafting Server on the same network can use them. At a glance Holds 16 cards Uses 2 FE a tick Counts toward the machine limit Without power, the network can't see the cards inside, so autocrafting stops. Jade shows how many cards a rack holds. Need more than 16 recipes? Add another rack. Recipe

Advanced Chips Rare versions of the Logic, Memory and Link Chip. Only the Chip Workshop makes them: every chip it finishes has a small chance of coming out Advanced. Critter Chance by default Basic Bitling 2% Logic, Memory or Link Bitling 5% Nibbling 15% Byteling its switch picks Advanced What they are for Top-tier recipes: Elite and Ultimate Decks and Crafting Decks, the biggest wafers, the 64K Storage Module, the Elite Data Cable, the Elite Generator and Processor, the Ultimate Archive, both Bays and the Dimension Upgrade. Seven of them round a Nibbling grow it into a Byteling. One of each, with a Data Crystal, builds a Synapse Core. A wild Bitling accepts one as a gift, like any other chip.

Synapse Core The key to the two biggest sizes of every wafer. A Byteling builds it in the Chip Workshop. At a glance Needs an Advanced Logic, Memory and Link Chip and a Data Crystal Builder a Byteling of any type Time 3,000 ticks, two and a half minutes Cost 50,000 FE from the Byteling's battery Put the four ingredients in the grid in any order. A younger critter just says it needs a Byteling. What it unlocks The 256K and 1M Capacity Wafers, the 128 and 256 Type Wafers, the 256K and 1M Fluid Capacity Wafers and the 64 and 128 Fluid Type Wafers. You upgrade to them like any other wafer, with the Cores in the crafting grid, and everything the old wafers hold comes along. Recipe

Deployment Bay A Deployment Bay places blocks, seeds and fluids from its own grid and tank into the space in front of it, as a player would. It can also throw items out. A Bitling in a hard hat does the work. At a glance Speed 2 seconds, down to half a second with 3 Speed Upgrades Cost 20 FE for each block, fluid or stack Holds 10,000 FE and 16 buckets Good to know An Output Port fills it. It runs on cable power and doesn't take up a place on the machine limit. With a Redstone Upgrade it can work once for each redstone pulse. In drop mode it pauses while 32 entities are near, so it can't flood a spot with items. Its opposite is the Demolition Bay. Recipe

Data Crystal The Data Crystal is JASM's basic material. You grow it on Seeded Amethyst. Mine a full cluster for Data Crystals, with your hand or any tool. Fortune gives more. Cut one into a Blank Chip at a Stonecutter. Four make a Wrench. One goes into a Synapse Core, which a Byteling builds in the Chip Workshop. Hand one to a wild Bitling and it follows you for about 30 seconds. With a book, it makes the JASM Guide.

Networks Machines that are joined by Data Cables form a network. So do JASM machines that simply touch each other, with no cable at all. What counts as a machine A network can only hold so many machines. The Network Brain page has the numbers. Everything that does a job counts: Encoding Terminals, Recipe Racks and Crafting Servers. Access Ports and every other port. Archives. Chip Workshops, Crystal Foundries, Crystal Resonators and Bitling Stations. Cables, generators, Creative Batteries, brains and chambers don't count. Neither do the two bays. A row of five Archives side by side is a network of five. Who may use it The network belongs to the player who set it up. The owner can trust other players at an Encoding Terminal. Trusted players can use the blocks and Archives on that network. Different players' networks never join. See co-op play for everything you can share. Seeing the network A linked Deck has a Network tab. It lists every machine, as a list or a branching tree, with where it is and whether it works. Power Cables carry power too. See power.

Crafting Server The Crafting Server does the work. It runs one crafting job at a time. Processors decide how many crafts run at once, and Storage Modules decide how big a job fits. At a glance Slots 4 for Processors, 4 for Storage Modules Uses 20 FE a tick, plus its Processors Each craft takes half a second, whatever the Processor Counts toward the machine limit Good to know Its parts are locked in while it works. Broken, it spills whatever its job held. With several servers on a network, a job goes to one that fits and is free. The screen shows what the job is waiting for: power, a card, a machine, space or the Deck. A job can be cancelled. What is left comes back. How a craft runs See autocrafting. Recipe

Crafting rules A rule makes the network craft for you, without you asking. Set them on the Rules tab of a Crafting Deck. Two kinds Rule Example Fewer than when I have fewer than 16 torches, craft 32 Every every minute, craft 8 bread Pick the item by holding it and clicking. A timer can be no shorter than 10 seconds by default. Where it goes Choose where the results go: onto the Deck, or straight into your inventory. A "fewer than" rule counts what you carry when it sends to you. Good to know A rule runs one job at a time. If a job can't start, the rule waits 5 seconds and tries again. The rule's line says why. Each rule can be switched on or off. The rules need the same chain as autocrafting: recipe cards, a rack, a server.

Seeded Amethyst Seeded Amethyst is a Block of Amethyst with a Crystal Seed in it. It grows Data Crystal buds on its open sides, like budding amethyst. Buds grow in four steps: Small Data Crystal Bud, Medium Data Crystal Bud, Large Data Crystal Bud, then a full Data Crystal Cluster. Mine the cluster for Data Crystal. Fortune gives more. A bud broken early gives Crystal Dust instead. Each time a bud grows, the block may wear down: Seeded, Worn Seeded Amethyst, Cracked Seeded Amethyst, then a plain Block of Amethyst. Mined at any stage, it gives the Block of Amethyst back and the seed is lost. A powered Crystal Resonator makes it grow faster. Growing crystals draw wild Bitlings. See befriending them. More in Growing Data Crystals.

Bitlings Bitlings are small robot helpers that work the Chip Workshop. Without one, a Workshop does nothing. Basic Bitling You can't craft one. Find a wild Bitling and hand it a chip. Makes Logic, Memory and Link Chips evenly, and rarely an Advanced one. Battery of 50,000 FE. The Network Brain recipe needs one. Typed Bitlings Surround a Basic Bitling with 8 chips of one type in a crafting grid to get a Logic, Memory or Link Bitling. Mostly makes its own type, sometimes Advanced. Battery of 100,000 FE. Trains on every chip it makes, then grows into a Nibbling. Recipes

Dimension Upgrade A Deck works only in the Overworld until you give it this. Install one in the Deck's upgrade slot and it works in the Nether, the End and modded dimensions too. What else it covers The same limit applies to linked ports, crafting jobs and rules. They pause when the Deck, or its network, is outside the Overworld without the upgrade. The upgrade slot stays open, so you can always fix it. Sending items to a player in another dimension needs the upgrade on both Decks. See sending items. Recipe

Getting started Everything JASM stores lives on wafers. Put wafers in a Deck and carry it with you. Link the Deck to a powered Archive to keep backups, so a lost wafer can be rebuilt onto a blank one. To open this guide at any time, craft the JASM Guide. A first hour Grow Data Crystals on a block of amethyst. Cut them into chips by hand. Craft your first Capacity Wafer and a Starter Deck. Build a Chip Workshop and befriend a wild Bitling to work in it. Link Chips come only from there. How the tiers use the chips The first tier of every wafer, Deck, generator and cable is made from vanilla items. From there on, recipes use JASM's own chips. Every higher tier needs the tier below it, and nothing it holds is lost on the way up. Where next Mechanics: how the systems work. Items, blocks and machines: one page for each, with recipes.

Power Acceptor JASM blocks only take power from JASM generators, batteries and cables. The Power Acceptor is the way in for power from other mods. Put it between the other mod's power and a Data Cable or machine. It pulls FE from the power blocks next to it, takes FE that other mods push into it, and feeds the cables and machines it touches. At a glance Speed 10,000 FE a tick by default Direction in only; it never gives power back If you only need to charge a Deck, a Combustion Generator is simpler. Recipe

JASM Guide The JASM Guide is the book you are reading now. Right-click it to open the guide. Hold the guide key (G by default) over any item's tooltip to jump to that item's page. You don't need the book for this. Recipe

Bitling Station Put a Bitling, Nibbling or Byteling in a Bitling Station and a little living copy pops out. It walks, sprints, hops, looks about and lies down for a rest. Right-click it to pet it. Power The little Bitling is only a body. The critter's own battery pays for the walk: 5 FE a tick while it is out and about. When the battery drops to 5%, it walks home and sits on the pad. The station passes the power it gets straight into the critter's battery. Connect the station to a Data Cable network or put a generator next to it. Stuck on the way home, or out of charge? It teleports back onto the pad. Good to know The screen shows what it is doing, its battery and a slider for how far it may roam (4 to 16 blocks). If something knocks it out, it comes back after 30 seconds with full health. Take the critter out and the little Bitling is gone. Hoppers and pipes can't reach the critter slot. Only the owner and the players they trust can open the station. A Bitling Station counts toward a network's machine limit. Recipe

Access Port The Access Port is how your network talks to other machines. Put one next to a furnace, a modded machine or a multiblock, and write processing cards for it. Every block touching the port that takes items counts as a machine. Setting it up Join the port to your network with a Data Cable. Write a processing card for it at an Encoding Terminal: what goes in, and up to three things that come back. Make the machine give its results back into the port, or use a hopper or a pipe. Jobs send the ingredients in and wait for the results to come back. Fluids work too. Choose several machines and the work is shared between them. Two shapes Full block: also takes items from any face, even without a crafting job. It has an eight-slot buffer. Ordinary items go to the owner's paired Deck, or to another paired Deck you pick in the port. Items wait if the Deck is full. Thin: a cable attachment, up to six on one cable, one per face. It can also sit straight on a machine with no cable. It stays off the network until you place a cable into its space. Convert one into the other in a crafting grid. Both recipes are below. Good to know A thin port serves and accepts items only through its outward face, including from pipes and hoppers while idle. Blocking mode waits to send new ingredients while the machine still holds some for this recipe. Add a Power Upgrade to supply FE to the machine it faces. It uses 2 FE a tick and counts toward the machine limit. Recipes

Fluid Capacity Wafers The same idea as a Capacity Wafer, for fluids. It holds any mix of fluids, counted in buckets: one bucket takes the room of one item. Wafer Holds, in buckets Needs Basic 256 vanilla items only 1K 1,024 Memory Chip 4K 4,096 Memory Chip 16K 16,384 Memory Chip and Link Chip 64K 65,536 Advanced Memory Chip 256K 262,144 Synapse Core 1M 1,048,576 Synapse Core Every size is made from three wafers of the size below. They are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their fluid and starts unlinked. The 256K and 1M sizes need Synapse Cores. Using them They go in any Deck slot, next to item wafers. The Deck's grid shows items and fluids together. A button shows only one kind. Right-click the grid with a full bucket, or shift-right-click it in your inventory, to pour it in. Click a fluid with an empty bucket to fill it. Input and Output Ports move fluids too. See item ports. Recipes
Crystal Dust Crystal Dust is what a bud gives when you break it before it is fully grown. Four dust and a redstone make a Crystal Seed. Buds are the early stages of Seeded Amethyst. Recipe

Archives An Archive keeps a backup of your wafers. If one is ever lost or destroyed, the Archive rebuilds it onto a blank wafer, items and all. Tier Wafers it protects Charge Uses Basic 3 50,000 FE 5 FE a tick Advanced 6 100,000 FE 10 FE a tick Ultimate 12 200,000 FE 20 FE a tick An Archive needs power to link or recover, so give it a cable or a generator next to it. Linking a wafer costs 1,000 FE and a recovery 10,000 FE by default. Using one Put a wafer in the link slot and press Link. Shift-right-click with the linked Deck to back up all its wafers in slot order. To recover a lost wafer, put a blank one of the same kind in the recover slot and press Recover. The blank wafer has to be the same size or bigger than the one it replaces. Upgrading The old Archive is used up. The new one keeps its links, its owner and its charge. Recipes

Network Brain A network holds only 4 machines on its own. A Network Brain lifts that to 12, and with Network Chamber s round it, a lot more. Brain Machines Uses each tick Holds No brain 4 Lone brain 12 8 FE 50,000 FE 1 floor 36 24 FE 145,000 FE 2 floors 54 52 FE 310,000 FE 3 floors 80 110 FE 660,000 FE 4 floors 120 240 FE 1,450,000 FE 5 floors 175 510 FE 3,050,000 FE 6 floors 260 1,100 FE 6,600,000 FE 7 floors 385 2,300 FE 13,800,000 FE 8 floors 576 5,000 FE 30,000,000 FE The rules Add a machine past the limit and the whole network stops, until you remove one or add a brain. A brain uses power every tick, and a taller tower uses more. If it runs out, the network falls back to 4 machines. A whole tower shares one pool of power. A cable on any of its floors or chambers fills it, and its screen shows the pool and what the tower uses each tick. Mined, a brain keeps its charge. Several brains on one network don't add up. Only the best one leads, the one with the most floors, then the one placed first. The machines' screens, Jade and a linked Deck's Network tab say when a network is full. See what counts as a machine. Floors and towers Put 8 Network Chambers round a brain on the same layer to make a floor. Stack floors into a tower. All of that is on the Network Chamber page. Recipe The recipe needs a Basic Bitling. Befriend a wild one first.

Autocrafting Ask for anything from your Crafting Deck, and the network crafts what it needs first. Here is the chain, start to finish. What you need A Crafting Deck, paired at an Encoding Terminal. Recipe Cards for the recipes, kept in a Recipe Rack. A Crafting Server with a Processor and a Storage Module. A Data Cable network that joins them, with power. For a machine instead of a crafting table, add an Access Port. Asking for something Open the Craft tab on the Deck, pick an item and an amount, and press Craft. The Deck works out the steps and shows: Makes: what you get. Crafts first: the steps in between, as a list or a tree. Missing: anything it can't find. A hammer in the Items tab marks items with a known recipe, even when some are already stored. While it runs Requested items come back as each batch finishes. Items made along the way stay with the job until it ends. A job list on the Deck shows every job. Click one to open its server from anywhere. Cancel a job and what is left comes back. When it says no The Deck tells you why: Missing ingredients. No Recipe Card makes that. No server with a Processor, or every fitting server is busy. The job is too big for the Storage Modules. The network is full. Add a Network Brain. The biggest request is 100,000 items. See also crafting rules.

Speed Upgrade Makes a port or a bay work faster. A port has four upgrade slots, one Speed Upgrade in each. Four of them move 96 items every operation, up from 1. See item ports. A Deployment Bay or Demolition Bay takes them too. Each upgrade shortens its action, down to half a second. Upgrades stack normally in your inventory and in storage. Recipe

Crystal Seed A Crystal Seed turns a Block of Amethyst into Seeded Amethyst, which grows Data Crystal. Use it on a Block of Amethyst. The seed is used up (not in creative mode). The Crystal Foundry also takes seeds, and makes Blank Chips from them. You can make a seed from amethyst, copper and redstone, or from four Crystal Dust and a redstone. More in Growing Data Crystals. Recipes

How storage works Your items don't sit inside a wafer. The wafer is a key, and the items live in the world's records under that wafer's number. That is why a wafer is safe to carry, and why it can be rebuilt. The pieces Wafers hold the items. See Capacity and Type Wafers. Decks carry the wafers and give you a screen to use them. See Decks. Archives keep backups, so a lost wafer can be recovered. See Archives. Safe by design A copied wafer stops working. It is wiped blank, and the original is untouched. A wafer that is older than the records say, or from another world, is locked. It keeps its contents and does nothing until it can be matched up again. A crash never duplicates items. Items from a mod you removed are kept until the mod comes back. What a wafer won't take Items that hold other items, like a full shulker box. Items that carry too much data to save. Items that can't be saved at all. The Deck's screen says why when it turns something away.

Sending items to players Deck to Deck sends items to another player on your network. They travel for a while, then land in the other player's inbox. How to send Pair your Deck at an Encoding Terminal. Press Deck to Deck on the Deck's screen and choose a player. Only players online on this network show up. Put the items in the send grid and press Send. The grid is 1 slot on a Starter Deck, 3 on a Basic, 6 on an Advanced and 9 on Elite and Ultimate. The trip At a glance Charge twice what the same items would cost to move Travel time 5 seconds, plus about 1 second for every 64 blocks Other dimension 30 seconds more Longest trip 3 minutes Trips at once 10 Changed your mind? Call back turns the trip round and brings the items to your own inbox. The inbox Items land in the inbox. Store all moves them onto your Deck. If the inbox is full, the trip waits there until there is room. Sending to another dimension needs a Dimension Upgrade on both Decks.

Storage Port A Storage Port lends the chest, tank or cauldron in front of it to the whole network. Everything inside shows up in a linked Deck next to the wafers, marked with a small chest. Take it out or put it in like wafer storage. Settings Filter: Item, Fluid, Tag and Mod ID. Access: read and write, read only or write only. Priority: higher priority takes things in first and the lowest is emptied first. Wafers go first on a tie. Anyone allowed on the network can use it. Recipe A Storage Port is an Access Port with a chest, a Link Chip and purple dye.

Combustion Generators Burn anything a furnace burns and get power. A generator sends it into every block it touches, and charges Decks and other chargeable items in its charging slot. Tier Burns Makes Holds Gives per block Basic 2x faster 40 FE a tick 100,000 FE 1,000 FE a tick Advanced 4x faster 160 FE a tick 400,000 FE 2,500 FE a tick Elite 8x faster 640 FE a tick 1,000,000 FE 5,000 FE a tick A piece of coal gives 32,000 FE in a Basic generator over 40 seconds, 64,000 FE over 20 seconds in an Advanced one and 128,000 FE over 10 seconds in an Elite one. Tips Put one next to a Chip Workshop or an Archive to power it without any cable. Drop a Deck in the charging slot to top up its battery. Jade shows how long the fuel has left. Upgrading The old generator is used up. The new one keeps its stored power. Recipes

Co-op play Friends can share one network. Everyone keeps their own Deck and their own wafers, while the network shares its machines, recipes and chests. This page covers every way to play together. Who owns what A network belongs to the player who set it up. A machine or cable placed onto it joins it and belongs to the network's owner, whoever placed it. Two players' networks never join. A cable placed between them stays on its own. Trusting friends Open an Encoding Terminal on your network. Open its Access window and type a friend's name. They don't have to be online. Stop trusting takes them off the list again. Only the owner can trust players, up to 32 per terminal. Trusted players can open and use every JASM machine and Archive on that network. Everyone else is turned away, even if they join a cable to it. Pairing your own Deck Each trusted player pairs their own Deck at the terminal, in the Deck Link window. It is one Deck per player: pairing another replaces your old one. A paired Deck gets the Network tab, autocrafting, ports and Deck to Deck. What you share and what you keep Shared by everyone Your own Recipe Cards, Recipe Racks and Crafting Servers the wafers in your Deck chests and tanks behind Storage Ports your Deck's charge the machine limit and the power your inbox Crafting together A craft started from your Deck takes its ingredients from your own wafers, and the result comes back to you. The recipes, racks, servers and processors belong to the network, so everyone crafts with the same setup. See autocrafting. Ports Item Ports and full Access Ports work with the owner's Deck at first. A trusted player can put their own paired Deck in the port's Deck Link window, and the port works with that Deck instead. Archives On a network, an Archive backs up the owner's Deck. The owner can link a trusted player's paired Deck instead. Only that player can then back up and recover; the other trusted players can look. Picking another player clears the backups. See backups and recovery. Sending items Deck to Deck sends items to any online player whose Deck is paired on the same network. See sending items to players. Good to know The Network tab shows the same machines to everyone who is trusted. JASM doesn't stop other players breaking your blocks. On a public server, use a land claim mod for that.

Backups and recovery Link a wafer to an Archive and it can come back from the dead. Here is how a backup lives and how to use it. Backing up Place an Archive and give it power. Shift-right-click it with your Deck. The Deck's wafers are backed up in slot order. Wafers already backed up on the network are skipped, and the Archive's free slots decide how many fit. The screen shows how many wafers are backed up. Recovering Put a blank wafer of the same kind in the recover slot and press Recover. The new wafer gets everything the lost one held. It has to be the same size or bigger. Who can use an Archive A standalone Archive works for its owner with no Encoding Terminal. It links the Deck in the owner's hand on the first backup. On a network, it defaults to the network owner. The owner can pick another trusted player's Deck instead. Trusted players can look at the backups. Replace a lost Deck for the same player and the backups stay.

Type Wafers A Type Wafer holds only a few kinds of item, but a huge amount of each. Pick one for the things you collect by the thousand, like cobblestone. Wafer Each type holds Needs 4 types 2,048 vanilla items only 8 types 8,192 Memory Chip 16 types 32,768 Memory Chip 32 types 131,072 Link Chip 64 types 524,288 Advanced Memory Chip 128 types 2,097,152 Synapse Core 256 types 8,388,608 Synapse Core What counts as a type A type follows vanilla stacking. Items that don't stack, like tools and armour, each take a whole type to themselves. Save the Type Wafers for stackable things. Upgrading Every size is made from two wafers of the size before. They are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their items and starts unlinked. The 128 and 256 sizes need Synapse Cores. For fluids, see Fluid Type Wafers. Recipes

Chip Workshop Put a Bitling in the Chip Workshop and feed it Blank Chip s. It turns them into Logic, Memory and Link Chip s, and now and then a rare Advanced Logic Chip. At a glance Single mode one chip every 10 seconds Batch mode up to 8 chips at once, in 60 seconds Cost 2,000 FE from the Bitling's battery for every chip Input a 2x2 grid Who makes what Critter Makes Basic Bitling all three types evenly, rarely an Advanced one Logic, Memory or Link Bitling mostly its own type, sometimes Advanced Logic Nibbling only its own type, Advanced more often Logic Byteling only its own type; a switch picks standard or Advanced Power The Workshop itself uses no power. Only the critter does. Power from a cable or a generator next to it goes straight into the critter's battery, and each chip takes some out. With no power at all, the critter keeps going until its battery runs flat, then naps until it is charged again. You can also charge a critter in a Combustion Generator. Building things in the grid Blank Chips can go in any of the four slots, and the critter keeps making chips even with other things beside them. A few things aren't chips: a Byteling builds the Synapse Core from what is in the grid. A Chip Workshop counts toward a network's machine limit. Recipe

Redstone Upgrade Lets redstone switch a port on and off. Install it in an Input, Output or Input Output Port. The mode button then picks one of three: Ignore redstone. Run while powered. Run while unpowered. The mode controls both directions at once. Take the upgrade out and the port runs normally again. Good to know All ports in the same block space get the same redstone signal. Each one follows its own mode. A port with no upgrade keeps running. The bays can use it to work once for each redstone pulse. Access Ports don't take this upgrade. Recipe

Item ports Ports mount on a Data Cable and move items and fluids between the network and the block next to them. Port Does Input Port pulls into a linked Deck Output Port pushes out of the Deck Input Output Port both, with output first Filters Each direction has an ordered list of filters: Item, Fluid, Tag and Mod ID. Empty input filters accept everything. Empty output filters send nothing. Speed Ports run twice a second while they are busy, and check once a second after five idle seconds. Four slots take Speed Upgrades. Upgrades Items per operation Items per second 0 1 2 1 4 8 2 16 32 3 48 96 4 96 192 Fluids share that speed with items. More slots A Power Upgrade makes the port supply FE to the machine it faces. A Redstone Upgrade makes it follow a redstone signal. Recipes An Input or Output Port is an Access Port with a hopper or dropper, a Link Chip and a dye.

Crystal Foundry The Crystal Foundry grows Data Crystals in bulk and cuts each one into a Blank Chip. One Crystal Seed makes 16 Blank Chips by default, one every 10 seconds. That is about 160 seconds a seed, and more than a seeded block gives on average. It runs on power like any other machine, from a Data Cable network or a generator next to it. It uses 40 FE each tick while it grows. The seed is used up as soon as it starts growing. Hoppers and pipes can put seeds in and take chips out. It counts toward a network's machine limit. See the Network Brain. Recipe

Processors Processors go in a Crafting Server. Each one runs crafts side by side, so more Processors means a job finishes sooner. Processor Crafts at once Adds to the server's use Basic 1 10 FE a tick Advanced 4 30 FE a tick Elite 16 80 FE a tick Every tier crafts at the same speed. A higher tier just does more of them at once. One Processor also handles a processing job: it keeps one set out in a machine until the results come back. With all Processors busy, a job waits, even if other machines are free. Making one Each tier is made from four of the tier below. The Advanced Processor also needs a Link Chip and the Elite an Advanced Logic Chip. Recipes

Blank Chip A Blank Chip is a Data Crystal cut flat. Every other chip starts as one. The Crystal Foundry makes them straight from Crystal Seeds. Cook one to start a Logic or Memory Chip. See Making chips by hand. A Bitling in the Chip Workshop turns Blank Chips into Logic, Memory and Link Chips, and sometimes Advanced ones. See Chip Workshop. Recipe

Items, blocks and machines One page for each item, block and machine, with its recipe. Hold the guide key over an item to jump to its page. The pages are in the order you will meet them. Crystals and chips JASM Guide: the book you are reading. Crystal Seed: turns amethyst into a crystal farm. Seeded Amethyst: where Data Crystals grow. Data Crystal: the raw material. Crystal Dust: what a bud broken early leaves. Crystal Resonator: makes crystals grow faster. Crystal Foundry: grows crystals in bulk. Blank Chip: cut from a Data Crystal. Logic and Memory Chips: the parts of every recipe. Bitlings and the Workshop Chip Workshop: a Bitling turns Blank Chips into better ones. Bitling Station: a home for your Bitling. Bitlings: the helpers. Nibblings and Bytelings: the grown-up stages. Link Chip: for the third tier. Advanced Chips: rare, for the top tier. Synapse Core: unlocks the biggest wafers. Storage Capacity Wafers: any mix of items. Type Wafers: a few kinds, in bulk. Fluid Capacity Wafers: any mix of fluids. Fluid Type Wafers: a few fluids, in bulk. Decks: the handheld reader. Crafting Decks: a Deck with a crafting grid. Dimension Upgrade: use a Deck outside the Overworld. Archives: backups for your wafers. Network and power Data Cables: join machines and carry power. Power Acceptor: lets other mods' power in. Combustion Generators: burn fuel for power. Network Brain: lifts the machine limit. Network Chamber: builds brain floors and towers. Ports and bays Access Port: talks to other machines. Item ports: move items and fluids in and out of a Deck. Storage Port: lends a chest or tank to the network. Speed Upgrade, Redstone Upgrade and Power Upgrade. Deployment Bay: places blocks and fluids. Demolition Bay: breaks blocks. Wrench: turn machines and pick them up. Autocrafting Encoding Terminal: writes recipes and pairs Decks. Recipe Cards: hold one recipe each. Recipe Rack: stores 16 cards. Crafting Server: runs the jobs. Processors: how many crafts run at once. Storage Modules: how big a job fits.

Recipe Cards A Recipe Card holds one recipe for autocrafting. Write it at an Encoding Terminal, then store it in a Recipe Rack. An empty card has nothing on it. One craft makes 4. A filled card shows what it makes, and what it takes. A card can hold a crafting recipe, or a processing recipe for a machine behind an Access Port. A filled card on its own in a crafting grid turns back into an empty one. The tooltip tells you whether a card is shaped or shapeless, what goes in, and what comes back. Recipe

Network Chamber Put 8 Network Chambers round a Network Brain, on the same layer, and it becomes a brain floor: a little glass office where 8 Bitlings work round a glowing core. Each floor lets the network hold more machines. Towers Stack floors straight on top of each other to make a tower. Every floor needs its own brain in the middle and all 8 of its chambers. A floor with a gap doesn't count, and splits the tower in two. A tower can be 8 floors tall. Floors stacked higher make a tower of their own. A tower shares one pool of power and uses more of it for every floor. Without power the Bitlings nap. Using a tower Cables can join any block of a tower, and a cable on any block powers the whole tower. Right-click any chamber or brain of a tower to open its screen. Chambers don't count toward the machine limit. Recipe One craft makes 4 chambers.

Crafting Decks A Deck with a 3x3 crafting grid. Ingredients come straight from its wafers, and the grid refills itself after every craft. Shift-click the result to craft as many as fit in your inventory. When you close it, the grid goes back into the wafers. It is also how you ask for autocrafting, and where you set crafting rules. Only Advanced, Elite and Ultimate Decks come in this form. Getting one Craft a Deck of the same tier, or upgrade from the Crafting Deck below it. Either way it keeps its wafers, its charge and whatever is in its grid. A new Crafting Deck links itself to the network of the Encoding Terminal you used last. Recipes

Power Most JASM blocks run on FE. Here is where it comes from and how it travels. Where it comes from Combustion Generators burn fuel. They are the simple answer. Other mods, through the Power Acceptor. JASM blocks never take power straight from another mod. How it travels A generator pushes power into every block it touches. Data Cables carry it through a network, each at its own speed. A slower cable slows what passes through it. A machine that touches a generator needs no cable. What uses it Block Uses Encoding Terminal 5 FE a tick Recipe Rack 2 FE a tick Crafting Server 20 FE a tick, plus its Processors Access Port 2 FE a tick Network Brain 8 FE a tick alone, 24 with one floor, up to 5,000 with 8 floors Crystal Resonator 10 FE a tick Crystal Foundry 40 FE a tick while it grows Archive 5, 10 or 20 FE a tick by tier Decks and Bitlings have their own batteries. Moving an item through a Deck costs 1 FE. All of these are the defaults, and the config can change them.

Storage Modules A job needs room for its ingredients and for everything it makes along the way. That room comes from Storage Modules in the Crafting Server. Module Items of a job 1k 1,000 4k 4,000 16k 16,000 64k 64,000 A server has four module slots, and their room adds up. If a job doesn't fit, the Deck says no server has enough modules. Making one Each size is made from the one below it. 4k needs a Memory Chip, 16k a Link Chip too, and 64k an Advanced Memory Chip. Recipes

Decks A Deck is a handheld reader for your wafers. Put wafers in its side panel and store or take items through the grid, with search, sorting and a few sizes of window. Tier Wafer slots Battery Starter 1 10,000 FE Basic 3 25,000 FE Advanced 6 50,000 FE Elite 12 125,000 FE Ultimate 24 250,000 FE Power Moving an item in or out costs 1 FE by default. Browsing is free. Without charge, a Deck can't move anything. Charge it in a Combustion Generator or anything else that charges items. What a Deck can do Hold item and fluid wafers side by side. Right-click a wafer to set its filters and priority. Link to a network at an Encoding Terminal, to receive port deliveries and see the Network tab. Send items to other players. Work outside the Overworld with a Dimension Upgrade. Upgrading The old Deck is used up. The new one keeps its wafers and its charge. Advanced and above also come as a Crafting Deck. Recipes

Encoding Terminal The Encoding Terminal writes recipes onto Recipe Cards. It is also where a Deck gets paired with a network, which unlocks autocrafting, ports and the Network tab. Writing a recipe Click items into the grid. They are only examples and are never used up. Put an empty or filled Recipe Card in. Press Encode. Take the finished card out first, or it can't write the next one. For a machine, choose it in the terminal's machine list first. Then fill the right-hand column with what the machine gives back. Scroll over a slot to change its amount, with Shift for bigger steps. Right-click with a full bucket or tank to set a fluid. See the Access Port. The Deck tab shows what is on your Deck. Click an item there for a copy to put in the grid. Nothing leaves the Deck. Pairing a Deck Open the Deck Link window with the side key. Put a Deck in its left slot and take it from the right. Pairing another Deck replaces that player's previous one. Who may use it The Access window lets the owner trust other players by name, up to 32. Trusted players share recipes but use their own stored items. At a glance Uses 5 FE a tick Counts toward the machine limit Recipe

Fluid Type Wafers A few kinds of fluid, each in bulk. Good for water, lava and the other fluids you pump all day. Like a Type Wafer, but for fluids. Wafer Each fluid holds, in buckets Needs 2 fluids 4,096 vanilla items only 4 fluids 16,384 Memory Chip 8 fluids 65,536 Memory Chip 16 fluids 262,144 Link Chip 32 fluids 1,048,576 Advanced Memory Chip 64 fluids 4,194,304 Synapse Core 128 fluids 16,777,216 Synapse Core Every size is made from two wafers of the size before. They are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their fluid and starts unlinked. The 64 and 128 sizes need Synapse Cores. For mixed fluids with no limit on kinds, see Fluid Capacity Wafers. Recipes

Training Bitlings A Bitling that works in the Chip Workshop learns from every chip it makes. When its training bar is full, you can grow it up in a crafting grid. The ladder Stage Chips to fill the bar Grows up with Basic Bitling none 8 chips of one type Logic, Memory or Link Bitling 100 7 chips of its type and a Diamond Nibbling 300 7 Advanced chips of its type and a Netherite Scrap Byteling top of the ladder nothing more Put the critter in the middle of the grid and the rest round it. It keeps its charge when it grows up. The real grids are on the pages for Bitlings and Nibblings and Bytelings. Why bother Bigger batteries: 50,000 FE for a Basic Bitling, 100,000 for a typed one, 200,000 for a Nibbling and 400,000 for a Byteling. Better odds of a rare Advanced chip. Only a Byteling can build a Synapse Core. The chip counts are the defaults and the config can change them.

Befriending Bitlings You can't craft a Basic Bitling. You find one in the wild and make friends with it. Where they live Well-lit grass in the Overworld. They turn up now and then. Never in oceans, rivers, beaches, deserts, badlands, mushroom fields, caves or the Deep Dark. They stay where they are, even when you walk away. Growing crystals draw them in. While you are near Seeded Amethyst, a Bitling sometimes wanders over for a look and stays around the crystals for a few minutes. None comes while another wild Bitling is close. Making friends Hand it a Logic, Memory or Link Chip. An Advanced one works too. It looks the chip over, nods and turns into a Basic Bitling item at its feet. Blank and unquenched chips only get a shake of the head. Hand it a Data Crystal instead and it eats the crystal and follows you for about 30 seconds. It stops if you get more than 24 blocks ahead. Hit one and it runs off. If it is knocked out, it vanishes in a puff and leaves nothing behind. What next Put your new Basic Bitling to work in the Chip Workshop, or train it into something bigger.

Logic and Memory Chips Logic and Memory Chips are the parts most JASM recipes are built from. A Logic Chip comes from an Unquenched Logic Chip: cook a Blank Chip on a Campfire, then drop it in water. A Memory Chip comes from an Unquenched Memory Chip: the same, but in a Blast Furnace. The whole stack cools at once, and no water is used up. Second-tier recipes need them, such as the Basic Deck and the 1K and 4K wafers. The Chip Workshop makes them too. Recipes

Crystal Resonator A powered Crystal Resonator makes the Seeded Amethyst next to it grow faster. It runs on power like any other machine, from a Data Cable network or a generator next to it. It uses 10 FE each tick by default. Every Seeded Amethyst touching it gets one extra growth attempt every 3.5 seconds (70 ticks) by default. Several Resonators add up. It gives no more crystals per seed, only sooner. Each extra growth has a 6% chance by default of wearing the block down. It counts toward a network's machine limit. See the Network Brain. Recipe

Capacity Wafers The simple storage chip. A Capacity Wafer holds any mix of items, up to a total. Put it in a Deck or link it to an Archive. Wafer Holds Needs Basic 256 items vanilla items only 1K 1,024 Memory Chip 4K 4,096 Memory Chip 16K 16,384 Memory Chip and Link Chip 64K 65,536 Advanced Memory Chip 256K 262,144 Synapse Core 1M 1,048,576 Synapse Core Upgrading Every size is made from three wafers of the size below. The three are used up, and the new wafer holds all of their items. It starts unlinked, so link it to an Archive again. Fluids have their own wafers: see Fluid Capacity Wafers. For a few item kinds in bulk, use a Type Wafer. Recipes

JASM: Just Another Storage Mod JASM is a digital storage mod built around storing your items and fluids on wafers, upgradeable chips that reside in your personal deck. Connect your Deck to a network of cables and machines, and every item on your wafers can be searched, crafted with and moved from one place. Start here Getting started: the first hour, and what each tier needs. Mechanics: how the systems work. Items, blocks and machines: one page for each, with recipes.

Growing Data Crystals Data Crystals are the raw material for everything in JASM. You grow them on a block of amethyst. Step by step Craft a Crystal Seed and use it on a Block of Amethyst. It becomes Seeded Amethyst. Buds grow on its open sides, like budding amethyst: small, medium, large, then a full Data Crystal Cluster. Mine the full cluster for Data Crystal, with your hand or any tool. Fortune gives more. A bud broken early gives Crystal Dust instead. Four dust and a redstone make a new seed. The seed wears out Each time a bud grows, the block may wear down one stage: Seeded, Worn, Cracked, then back to a plain Block of Amethyst. By default the chance is 12% for each bud. Mined at any stage, the block gives the Block of Amethyst back and the seed is lost. Growing faster A powered Crystal Resonator makes a block grow faster. For bulk, the Crystal Foundry turns each Crystal Seed straight into Blank Chips, with no Block of Amethyst to wear out. Visitors Growing crystals draw wild Bitlings. Find out more.
